short: Wholeness, a fresh start, the circle
body: Zero (零, líng) carries no strong homophone in Mandarin. It is read as wholeness and completion because of its round shape, and as a clean beginning. In prices and numbers it is neutral: it amplifies the digits in front of it (8,000 reads as a bigger 8) rather than adding meaning of its own.
use: Common in round prices and dates. Neutral in phone numbers; many buyers prefer fewer zeros in favour of 6, 8 and 9.

body: One (一, yī) stands for unity, beginnings and being first. When reading phone numbers aloud, Chinese speakers say 'yāo' for 1, which echoes 要 (yào, 'want / will'). That is why combinations like 168 (一路发, 'prosper all the way') and 1314 (一生一世, 'one life, one world') are so popular.
use: Positive in combinations: 168, 1314, 1688, 518. Alone it is mildly positive.

short: 'Good things come in pairs' (好事成双)
body: Two (二, èr) is lucky because of the proverb 好事成双 (hǎo shì chéng shuāng) — 'good things come in pairs'. Doubled characters such as 囍 (double happiness) appear at weddings, and gifts are often given in pairs. One caution: 二 is also slang for 'silly', as in 二百五 (250), so context matters.
use: Good for weddings, gifts and couples' numbers. Avoid 250 as a price.

short: Life and growth in Cantonese; can echo 'scatter' (散) in Mandarin
body: Three (三, sān) is close to 生 (shēng, 'life / birth') — especially in Cantonese — so it is linked with growth and vitality, and 3 marks key life stages (birth, marriage, death). In some Mandarin contexts it can echo 散 (sàn, 'to scatter / break up'), so couples sometimes avoid giving three of something.
use: Generally positive, especially with 8 (38, 'grow prosperous') and in 3344 (生生世世, 'life after life').

short: Sounds like 'death' (死) — the most avoided digit
body: Four (四, sì) sounds almost identical to 死 (sǐ, 'death'). This is the single strongest number taboo in Chinese-speaking regions: many buildings skip the 4th, 14th, 24th floors (tetraphobia), hospitals avoid room 4, and phone numbers or licence plates heavy in 4 sell at a discount. Combinations like 14 (要死, 'want to die') and 74 (气死) are especially disliked.
use: Avoid in prices, SKUs, addresses, floor numbers, phone numbers and gift quantities aimed at Chinese customers.

short: The Five Elements — or 'without' (无); 'me' (我) in slang
body: Five (五, wǔ) links to the Five Elements (五行: wood, fire, earth, metal, water) and to the emperor, so it has a dignified side. It can also sound like 无 (wú, 'without / nothing'), which is negative next to wealth digits (58 can read as 'no fortune'). In online slang 5 stands for 我 (wǒ, 'I / me') — the basis of 520 ('I love you').
use: Great in love slang (520, 521, 530). Mixed in business numbers.

sounds: 溜 liū / 流 liú (smooth, flowing)
short: Smooth, flowing success — 六六大顺 'everything goes smoothly'
body: Six (六, liù) sounds like 溜 (liū, 'smooth / slick') and 流 (liú, 'to flow'). The idiom 六六大顺 (liù liù dà shùn) wishes that 'everything goes smoothly'. Online, 666 (liù liù liù) is the most common way to say 'awesome / well played' in games, livestreams and comments. Businesses love 6 for smooth operations.
use: Excellent in business numbers, phone numbers, opening dates and domain names (666, 6666, 66666).

sounds: 起 qǐ (rise) / 齐 qí (together) / 气 qì (energy)
short: Rise and togetherness — with a Ghost Month caveat
body: Seven (七, qī) echoes 起 (qǐ, 'to rise / start') and 齐 (qí, 'together, complete'), and the Qixi Festival (七夕, the 7th day of the 7th lunar month) is China's Valentine's Day. The 7th lunar month is also Ghost Month, so some people avoid 7 for weddings or moves in that period. Overall it reads as positive — especially at the end of a strong sequence.
use: Positive after strong digits: 666667 reads as 'smooth, smooth… and rise'. Avoid scheduling launches in the 7th lunar month if your audience is traditional.

short: Prosperity — the luckiest number in Chinese culture
body: Eight (八, bā) sounds like 发 (fā), as in 发财 (fācái, 'to get rich'). It is the most sought-after digit: the Beijing Olympics opened at 8 pm on 8/8/2008, licence plates and phone numbers full of 8s sell for large sums, and prices ending in 8 are standard in retail. Its shape (two joined loops) also suggests continuity.
use: The #1 digit for prices, phone numbers, plates, addresses and launch dates.

short: Longevity and eternity (久) — the emperor's number
body: Nine (九, jiǔ) sounds like 久 (jiǔ, 'long-lasting, forever'), making it a favourite for weddings, anniversaries and long-term relationships. Historically nine was associated with the emperor — the Forbidden City uses nine-row door studs. 99 (久久) means 'forever and ever'.
use: Weddings, anniversaries, long-term contracts, 999 red-envelope amounts.

short: Not a taboo in China — some readings are positive
body: Thirteen has no traditional stigma in Chinese culture. Some people read it as 实生 ('assured growth'). In online slang 十三点 (shí sān diǎn) is a Shanghainese-origin tease meaning 'silly', but the plain number is fine. Western tenants may still avoid it, so international buildings sometimes skip both 4 and 13.
use: Fine for Chinese audiences; consider Western sensitivities for global brands.

body: Fourteen combines 1 (yāo, 'want / will') and 4 (death), so it reads as 要死 ('going to die') or 是死 ('is death'). Many residential towers in China and Hong Kong skip floor 14 as well as 4.
use: Never use in prices, SKUs, floors or plates for Chinese buyers.

body: 22 doubles the pair symbolism of 2 and is sometimes read as 易易 ('easy, easy'). It is a common choice for wedding dates and couple-related numbers.
use: Weddings, partnerships, couple products.

short: Double prosperity — also chat slang for 'bye-bye'
body: 88 doubles the luck of 8 (发发, 'prosper, prosper') and resembles 囍 (double happiness). Online, 88 (bā bā) is shorthand for 'bye-bye' in chats. It is one of the most common red-envelope amounts (¥88, ¥888).
use: Red envelopes, prices (¥88), phone endings, store numbers.

body: 99 reads as 久久 ('long, long time'), a wish for an eternal relationship or long-lasting business. The Double Ninth Festival (重阳节) on the 9th day of the 9th lunar month honours elders and longevity.
use: Anniversary gifts, wedding red envelopes (¥999, ¥9,999), subscription pricing.

body: 168 is read as 一路发 (yí lù fā) — 'fortune all along the road'. It is a favourite for business phone numbers, shop numbers and prices, and was famously used in the domain 168.com and in names of countless trading companies.
use: Business phone numbers, product prices (¥168), launch codes.

short: Laughing out loud — 'LOL' in Chinese chats
body: 233 means laughter, like 'LOL' or 'haha'. It comes from emoji code #233 on the forum Mop, a face pounding the floor with laughter. More 3s means more laughter: 23333333.
use: Comments, danmu (bullet comments) on video sites, social captions.

short: Calling someone a fool — never price at 250
body: 二百五 (èr bǎi wǔ, 250) is a well-known insult meaning a foolish or reckless person. Theories trace it to old coin strings (a 'half-string' of 500 coins). Pricing something at ¥250 or giving ¥250 in a red envelope would be read as an insult.
use: Never use as a price, gift amount or quantity.

body: 518 reads as 我要发 (wǒ yào fā) — 'I'm going to prosper'. It is a hugely popular business number, and May 18 is a favoured date for company openings in China.
use: Business phone numbers, opening dates (May 18), promo codes.

short: 'I love you' — May 20 is an online Valentine's Day
body: 520 (wǔ èr líng) sounds like 我爱你 (wǒ ài nǐ, 'I love you'). May 20 (5/20) has become an unofficial Valentine's Day in China: marriage registrations spike and couples send ¥520 or ¥520.20 red envelopes. 521 (5/21) is read as 'I do / I'm willing' (我愿意).
use: Romance marketing, gift pricing (¥520), couples' products, 5/20 campaigns.

body: 521 is read as 我愿意 ('I'm willing / I do') or also 'I love you'. It is the natural reply to 520, and May 21 is the second day of the online Valentine's pair.
use: Proposal and wedding marketing; couple sets priced 520/521.

body: 530 approximates 我想你 (wǒ xiǎng nǐ, 'I miss you'). It belongs to the same family of romantic number codes as 520 and 1314.
use: Long-distance relationship messages, gifting copy.

body: 555 imitates the sound of crying (呜呜呜, wū wū wū). It is used online to express sadness or mock-sadness, much like 'sob' or a crying emoji.
use: Chat and comments only — avoid for prices.

short: 'Awesome! Well played!' — the internet's favourite praise
body: In Chinese internet culture 666 means 'awesome / so smooth / well played'. It began in gaming (praising a skilful player) and spread to livestreams, short-video comments and everyday chat; people even write 6666666. The root is 溜 (liū, 'smooth, slick') and the traditional 六六大顺 ('everything goes smoothly'). For Western audiences it may evoke 'the number of the beast', so international brands should explain the Chinese meaning.
use: Praise, gaming, livestream culture; business numbers wishing smooth operations.

sounds: 去死吧 'go to hell / drop dead'
body: 748 sounds like 去死吧 (qù sǐ ba, 'go and die'). It is a rude insult online and a very bad choice for phone numbers, plates or prices despite containing an 8.
use: Avoid everywhere.

body: 886 reads as 拜拜了 (bài bài le, 'bye-bye then'). It is a casual sign-off in chats, alongside 88.
use: Chat sign-offs; playful marketing copy.

body: 888 triples the power of 8 (发发发). It is the classic lucky price, red-envelope amount and casino/shop number across Chinese-speaking markets and Chinese diaspora communities.
use: Premium prices, red envelopes (¥888), VIP phone numbers, promotions.

body: 996 refers to a work schedule of 9 am to 9 pm, six days a week, associated with parts of China's tech sector. It became a flashpoint for debates about overwork. It is not a luck number — it is social commentary.
use: Workplace and HR discussions; avoid as a cheerful brand number.

short: Eternity — forever and ever and ever
body: 999 intensifies 九/久 into 'eternal'. It is popular in wedding gifts (999 roses), anniversary pricing and brand names suggesting endurance.
use: Wedding red envelopes, 999 roses, anniversaries.

short: 'For a whole lifetime' — the 4 is forgiven here
body: 1314 reads as 一生一世 (yì shēng yí shì, 'one life, one lifetime'). It is one of the few combinations where the 4 is fully accepted, because the phrase is so romantic. 5201314 means 'I love you for a lifetime'.
use: Romantic gifts (¥1,314), wedding dates, jewellery pricing.

sounds: 一路发发 'prosper all the way, doubly'
body: 1688 extends 168 with a second 8: 'fortune all along the road, doubled'. It is extremely popular in company names, prices and trade platforms.
use: Business prices (¥1,688), store numbers, B2B brands.

body: 3344 approximates 生生世世 (shēng shēng shì shì, 'through every lifetime'). It is a romantic code where the 4s are accepted because of the phrase.
use: Romantic messages, wedding marketing.

body: 6666 is a stronger version of 666 — both 'extremely awesome' in slang and 'extremely smooth' in the traditional sense. Four-digit repeating numbers (AAAA) are among the most valuable patterns for phone numbers and plates.
use: VIP phone numbers, domain names, premium plates.

body: Five repeated 6s (AAAAA) signal overwhelming praise online and an exceptionally smooth path in traditional terms. As a 5-digit repeating .com it belongs to the rarest numeric domain class.
use: Status numbers; premium numeric domains.

py: liù liù liù liù liù qī
sounds: 溜溜溜溜溜 + 起 'smooth ×5, then rise'
short: Smooth, smooth, smooth… and RISE — the name of this site
body: 666667 reads as five 'smooth / awesome' sixes followed by 七 (qī), which echoes 起 (qǐ, 'rise'). It is an easy-to-remember, easy-to-type number with no 4 in it, which is exactly what Chinese-speaking users value in phone numbers and domains. A few fun facts: 666667 is a prime number, and 0.666667 is the six-decimal rounding of 2/3. We use it as a name only; it does not refer to any brand, product or organisation.
use: Brand name of this site; a memorable number with a positive sound.

body: 7456 approximates 气死我了 (qì sǐ wǒ le, 'I'm so angry / you're killing me'). It is used jokingly in chats.
use: Chat only.

body: 8888 is among the most valuable number patterns for plates, phone numbers and prices. Phone numbers ending in 8888 have sold for sums far above ordinary numbers in mainland China and Hong Kong auctions.
use: VIP numbers, flagship prices, premium domains.

py: wǔ èr líng yī sān yī sì
sounds: 我爱你一生一世 'I love you forever'
body: 5201314 combines 520 (I love you) and 1314 (for a whole lifetime). Couples send ¥52.01314-style transfers, and it is a common engraving and password-style code.
use: Romantic gifts, jewellery and wedding marketing.

body: 9999 intensifies longevity and eternity, and it is a common high-value wedding red envelope amount (¥9,999).
use: Wedding red envelopes, luxury anniversary pricing.

body: Beyond the spy reference, 007 in Chinese work slang means working 00:00 to 24:00, 7 days a week — an even more extreme version of 996.
use: Workplace commentary only.
